I love this game. It's got a lot of depth and content, and has a certain old-school-RPG feel that I love.

That being said, there are some easily fixable UI issues that drive me insane:
[list]
 [*] Left click to move / Right click to select feels backwards and is the opposite of AoE/Civ/etc. There should at least be an option to swap these. I get that some Mac users only have a left click but most gamers have both.
[*] There's no autosave (this is probably my biggest gripe).
[*] If you go to manually save and accidentally hit quit (next to it), that's it: your game is gone and you're looking at the desktop (there should be a confirmation prompt if we haven't recently saved).
[*] Manual save doesn't pre-fill a suggested save name, and if you save without specifying one it silently fails
[*] The UI doesn't clearly indicate who the active commander is. You get used to looking in the top left corner to confirm who is active but it's still possible to make mistakes. Some sort of active unit halo/circle would be nice.
[*] There's no way to select an entire column when transferring units in the army. It's either select the entire type or one-at-a-time.
[*] The sans-serif title screen font feels lazy. Can we at least have Times New Roman?
[/list]

The conquest of elysium series is by far the least fun set of games that I've played for cumulatively over 100 hours, and will likely continue to play.  The game itself offers such a unique and interesting set of possibilities and strategies that it is always tantalizing to try a new set of starting conditions.  Not only that but there are any number of unique encounters and enemy combinations which can keep the game fresh and exciting.  

Unfortunately the game does everything in it's power to stop you from experiencing any of it.  Between the extreme imbalance of classes, impenetrable resource barriers, terrain which constantly hinders your movement, and agonizingly long waiting times between turns there is rarely much of anything to actually do on a turn.  Generally speaking your commanders will have three action points per turn, but the vast majority of tiles require two or more action to move through, leaving you with one or two clicks for each turn before ending and waiting on opponents.  Then there is the winter season which makes all the tiles take even more points to traverse, meaning you might move on a turn then not even be able to act at all the next round.  Speaking of seasons the winter will also half your economy from many money making tiles.  That's a problem because the economy is another way the game halts your engagement.  Most classes who don't rely on gold exclusively will languish for resources, and have trouble being able to even recruit units.  In the event you can hire or summon your units they are often weak to the point of being laughable unless they are ludicrously expensive.   Sometimes these units are also problematic to summon as well, you might fail to summon them and have your whole army killed by the unit you summoned after a three hour game.  Or perhaps you will simply be punished by having your commander be unable to move for an indeterminate amount of turns.  Either option is basically punishing the player for trying to engage in the mechanics of the game.  

There are so many anecdotes I could list, constantly having groups of two snakes or a single deer take my resources, or having all my commanders only able to move one or less tiles per round due to weather and geography, or simply not being able to get any economy because every resource tile has massive NPC armies on it which lock me out of building an army.  

The list could go on, but the main takeaway is that this game doesn't want you to play it.  it has cool ideas and interesting classes with the foundation of a great game, but then the mechanics of it try at every turn to stop your fun.  There are a lot of people who play the game who I see enjoying the "difficulty" but for me the strategy of the game is very simple to understand, and would be fun to play if not for the constant barrage of annoyances and inconveniences.  Unfortunately there just isn't another game like it, and so I'll probably come back again and try to ignore the abuse the game puts me through to scrape what little fun from it that the game will let me have.  From what I've heard conquest of elysium 5 doesn't address any of these issues either, so I'm not hopeful that there will be a solution.  Do yourself a favor and just don't even play the game, don't get a taste of the poisoned fruit or you might get tricked into eating the whole thing like me.

The kind of game you really want to like, but it doesn't let you.

In theory this is right down my alley. Fantasy 4X-lite with randomized maps and starts, and a large variety of spells and creatures.

The problem is it manages to be annoying in all the areas that matter to make a "lite" game playable:

- UI is clumsy and non-standard: weird "right-click to select and left click to move" convention; Transfer screen has the genius idea to put X symbols on unit icons [thankfully fixed in CoE5] making them unreadable; there are few actions to do every turn yet they managed to bury them in menus.

- Lack of tooltips for some map symbols, for instance what does a catapult mean in a location's attributes? You won't know unless you stumbled upon the [i]textual description of the icon[/i] in the manual. [CoE5 introduces a key to look up tile details]

- UI for viewing units in an army or transferring them is *especially* clumsy: hard to differentiate tiny sprites, no summary of how many units of each type a commander has (except in a global window you have to scroll through) [CoE5 shows unit counds in the Transfer screen], and the display when multiple armies are standing on the same tile is a mess. Positive side: it'll make you appreciate the interface in every other 4X.

- Slow start where you need multiple turns and solid expansion to even purchase your first unit or cast your first ritual.

- Ironically there's a large variety of units and spells, but you'll be mostly repeating the same two summoning rituals over and over and using the same units for the whole game. Makes you miss the excitement of a neutral sometimes joining your ranks or the capture of a unit dwelling in HOMM or King's Bounty,

- No control or influence whatsoever on fights, which are exceedingly random: some of your commanders insist on leading from the front and will die in most serious fights; worse, a single lucky shot can kill your main commander that you spent hours leveling and pretty much end your game. This means you'd LIKE to play fast and loose because this is a "lite" game, but you CAN'T and you have to tediously micromanage instead which leaders participate in a fight, with a UI that slows the process down.

- The combat system changed from CoE3. Among the changes is the introduction of a massive amount of friendly fire, with mages and dragon breaths often damaging more of your own units than the enemies. Where in CoE3 a dragon or powerful mage was just a flat out cool addition to your army that you could enjoy, in this edition (and CoE5) you'll most often than not curse helplessly as your mage Decays to death your recent cool summon, or your dragon fries a dozen of your men while chasing a single remaining Feared enemy. Mitigations exist but are incomplete and micromanagement-heavy.

- No end of battle summary. With battles involving hundreds of units with tiny samey sprites, it's easy to lose track and not realise you lost a key unit in the mess. [There's a command line option to enable battle reports, but you have to use it when starting a game. Afterwards, it's too late to enable it.]

- No way to visualize how far your army can move along a path this turn? No way to set a path for an army over multiple turns!? Come on, Heroes of Might and Magic 1 had this in 1995. This means shuffling armies around mid-late game is really a pain.

- The Civ-like "barbarians"/independents are ramped up to 11, in power but especially in number of stacks spawned. Initially you might like the challenge, only to realise it's nigh-impossible to hold all the little resource points on the map without having dedicated armies playing whack-a-mole with bandits, or tediously placing sufficient garrisons on all of them. Seriously, where's the "lite" aspect at this point? Every "deep" game I can think of has less micromanagement in this area. [CoE5 lets you "overrun" puny stacks without combat, making the fly-swatting a tiny bit less grating]

- Dictatorial design decision to let you have multiple save slots, but not load them without returning to the desktop and restarting the game. Combine with the unpredictable fights, and you have a recipe for disaster. Games can last hours despite the supposed "lite" aspect, and who wants to restart and do the tedious start all over because the game decided to screw you? [CoE5 at least lets you resign and get back to the Main Menu...]

There is a multiplayer component, but I don't see myself playing my typical "3 players allied vs the AI" romp I do in most 4X games, since the game is likely to screw over and maim one of the players by killing its best commander, ending the coop fun for everyone. Same problem as in single player, only three times as likely with three players.

There are some positive points buried under this unsufferable UI and game design: large battles are impressive, creatures of various sizes allow for some epic and frightening monsters, some boasting spells of apocalyptic power. The maps have some interesting things to discover such as the lair of the dwarves which if unchecked can seriously impact the map, portals to go through. But the pain you have to go through to experience this doesn't seem worth it.

Last topic: unit and faction descriptions are sometimes decent. At other times they try to be humorous but are rather on the dumb side and fall flat for me, with nonsensical and possibly self-referential stuff like bears liking potatoes and teaming with deer to attack towns.

Along with Dwarf Fortess, Illwinter Games stand as the ultimate function-over-form brand of entertainment. So many mechanics and moving parts, so many different strategies and experiences to be had. While DF is the like Silmarillion and Dominions may be likened to The Lord of the Rings, this game is like The Hobbit: shorter and sweeter, less complex but still packed with flavor. 

The graphics are simplistic (the game was programmed by one person using SDL, with the art and lore by another), but if you're the kind of person who appreciates this kind of grandeur of depth in a game then this probably won't bother you too much. Kind of like a TRPG with minimal visual aids, barebones but immersive enough to spark the imagination.  

There's a lot of randomness but so much content that it makes it worth it. This isn't the kind of game where each playthrough is the same enemies in slightly different locations in functionally identical procedurally-generated rooms,  after playing COE for hundreds of hours you may still be encountering new enemies and events that you haven't seen yet, and all of this with *NO DLC* (Looking at you, Paradox). 

One of the least-conventional aspects of this game is the combat, once two armies clash, the computer takes control in an algorithmic autobattle format. The algorithm for the battles (along with all of the other mechanics) is actually listed in the manual, which I thought was very cool. The actual tactics used by the computer involve a lot of RNG, so the outcomes are hard to predict, simplifying the strategic element a bit but granting it a touch of cinematic tension (though sometimes frustrating; it has a strong roguelike flavor). 

In short, this game is as much of a story generator as a game, and a very good one. It's about halfway between Civilization and Dungeons and Dragons in that respect. The games are not symmetrical and very rarely fair, but they are still a blast nonetheless! I'm looking forward to COE5 in August B)

Also, if you appreciate pure strategy over roguelike randomness, the other series by Illwinter, "Dominions," is unparallelled!!

ユニット同士の大規模オートバトルが醍醐味の4Xグランドストラテジー。
基本は指揮官を操作し、野良ユニットと戦いながら土地を占領し、占領した土地から得たリソースを使ってユニットを雇用し、ユニットが溜まったら他の勢力を潰しに行く。Age of Wondersとかが近い。
勢力によって雇えるユニットもリソースの種類も経済の形式も全く異なるので、いろんな遊び方ができる。

■良い点
・大量のユニット同士のオートバトルを眺めていると楽しい。ほとんどのユニットは1x1だが、4x4とかの超巨大なやつもいたりしてロマンがある。
・勢力の数が異様に多い。フレーバーだけでなく経済の様式が全く異なるので、いろんな遊び方ができる。
・ユニットに超細かいスタッツとかが設定されていて、戦闘中の状態異常や負傷なども再現されていて、ファンタジー世界で軍を率いている解像度が高い。

■悪い点
・AIがアホ。メイン拠点を潰されるとゲームオーバーなのだが、拠点を空っぽにして占領されて勝手に滅亡したりする。なんもしてないのに敵が全部自滅して勝ったなんてことも。
・難易度設定はかなり雑で、AIの出力にゲタを履かせるだけ。最高難易度はおそらくプレイアブルでない。
・マップの種類によって相性が良すぎる文明とそうでない文明があり、そのへんのバランスが悪い。
・強い選択肢と弱い選択肢の格差が激しすぎる

I love Dominions.  I played 4 and 5.  I picked this up on sale when they announced that CoE 5 was coming.  This is not Dominions.  That is obvious but still worth saying.  

It lacks lots of little quality of life things that it should have.  The only way to exit the game is to quit.  Meaning that if you still want to play, just not this game because things have gone poorly or you don't like the way a race plays, you have to quit and restart the game.  You can't exit to the initial menu and start a new game.  For me this came up a lot.

When you buy troops, it will display all the locations you can buy them at and you can only buy at each location once per month.  Fine, except it doesn't tell you where any of the locations are.  You can buy at a guard tower but you can have a dozen guard towers.  They don't get names.  You can right click to center the screen on a purchase location (something it doesn't tell you but I kept fiddling) but the purchase screen is still over the map and covers 60% of the map.  If you have locations close together you can't see where you are purchasing.  In addition to this, purchasing defaults to your original base every time, no matter what commander is active.  This can lead to you purchasing troops at the back of your empire instead of at the front where they are needed.

Commanders don't stack or follow.  In Dominions you will have multiple commanders and casters in any army.  While you don't need specific leadership in this game (any mob will follow any commander in any number) you often need multiple commanders for magic support.  You have to move them all one at a time, with variable movement rates, sometimes leading to a caster with no troops going in alone because you didn't know the main army couldn't move this turn.

It plays much more randomly than Dominions.  Just watching the player notifications between turns you will see 50% of the players (all bots in my case not live people) die in the first dozen rounds.  This can be due to not guarding your base while you scrounge for resources in the early game or having your only commander (because you can't afford another for quite a while) die.

While the level of complexity is similar to Dominions the level of information provided to the player is not.  Casting is expensive but there is no list of spells available to help you decide what to aim for.  Are tier 3 worth it?  Have to experiment and find out, except resources are always scarce.  The bigger your empire the larger your front line.  There is never a time when you are flush.

The worst part is, it's not a bad game.  I still want to go back and try again, but it is really frustrating and could easily have been better with out significant change to content.  This is all about implementation.  I can only home that 5 learns some lessons from the disappointments of 4.

Conquest of Elysium 4 is a great game to play when you don't have internet or a mouse, perfect when you have a laptop and on a long train or plane ride.  The game can be treated like an adventure, set on discovering new tiles and monsters with their own lore. 

The game lacks a lot of elements that make it competitive, like being largely luck-based and having unbalanced classes, but there are ways to strategize and make efficient plays that can provide the player some advantage in multiplayer games or against AI. 

Although small, the community has uploaded mods that can be added to make gameplay more enjoyable, balanced, and favorable to the player's desire.

Multiplayer games can last well over 2 hours if its a 1v1, and can last well over 4 hours if its a 2v2. Patience is definitely required to enjoy the game.

It's a nice idea but it is definitely not as fun as Dominions.

A lot of Dominion fan-boys will probably piss on this review. Yet, it is the honest opinion of a strategy and RPG fan. The game feels like a non-optimized poorly executed student project that has ripped off all assets of the Dominions series, and despite all this, the game is enjoyable.

There is so much wrong with this game, the balance, the RPG progression elements, the AI, and the user friendliness of the game.

Balance:
•	Barbarian start with large army of weak troops. Perfect for fighting small animals like dear and can take on some bears. Massacred by larger creatures. Hero, which is needed to move the army on the world map is equally weak and stands in the front row. The strategy of barbarians resolves around gathering enough money to afford a spirit guide and play similar to any other spell casting hero in summon beings to do the fighting.
•	Trolls on the other hand, start with a massive troll hero, who can take on any low-, to mid-level creatures on its own. No army is needed, till you encounter larger creatures. In which case your troll hero reduces to a weak front row unit like the barbarian hero.
•	Starting location can differ tremendously, so every game is unbalanced between players from the very start.

RPG:
•	Progression is divided into four levels of experience. The bonuses of each level are fixed and very limited. While a +1 hitpoint is good for a low level unit, it is absolutely negligible for units with over 100 hitpoint at level 1. Also, a low level unit will probably not reach much farther than one or two levels before being hit in the face by a stray arrow.
•	Also, progression of caster units depends on the amount of resources you have. A starting witch may need a hundred turns to gain some experience levels, but a new apprentice witch starting when you bank is full of mushrooms can easily turn into a hag (highest caster level of the witch class) and summon several ancient hydra’s and other old ones in a few turns.

AI:
•	Roaming monsters do not stick to their habitat, nor behave like animals. Crab are found in mountain ranges instead of attacking coastal villages as its description suggests, dears wander off to desert areas where they do not suffer from thirst and giant sea dragons don’t seem to make up their mind to either raid your stronghold or go back to the deep sea where their lair is 
•	AI players can be wiped out on the first turn due to unbalancing starting locations and stupid decision making of the AI (like leaving their camp when a few boars stand next to their stronghold)

User friendly:
•	The lack of polish is noticed in every interface: When you start a game and have a very bad start you have to quit and restart the game, to find that all settings (like world, number of players, etc.) have been reset. You cannot rebind keys, cannot set multi-turn routes, it is often not clear why you are allowed to enter a 3-move forest with only a single action point available and not move at all during the next turn, selecting spell of your hero requires you to enter the army roster and click on your hero after you have found him, 

I would expect that in the fourth iteration of the game a lot of these problems would have been addressed. Fortunately, most issues are not game breaking in the single player experience. The unbalanced aspects can actually be used to set the difficulty of the game (however, there is no clear and logical ordering of the difficulties each class represent). The AI problems of other AI players can also be somewhat overcome by playing multiple factions yourself. This also disables the problem that you accidently finish the game by eliminating the last group of AI units, and thus allows you to explore other planes.
